# Chalk And 17 Other NPM Packages Compromised In Supply-Chain Attack

Darren Meyer

Darren Meyer 

Security Research Advocate

September 8, 2025

9 min. read

The maintainer of the well-known ``chalk`` package (known as “qix”) reports that they believe their NPM account was targeted to replace several packages with malicious equivalents, posing a supply-chain attack vector for any users of the packages. At the time of writing, the following packages are affected by this 0-day malware: [...] The above NPM packages were edited to include malware. The malware runs when a user visits a page containing one of the compromised versions, injecting itself into common JavaScript facilities within users’ browsers. It watches for sensitive payment data, focusing on cryptocoin transactions (including Etherium, Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash, Litecoin, etc.), and replaces the destination data. Since this tampering occurs before the transactions are signed, this effectively steals the payment to the [...] These malicious packages are flagged in the Checkmarx Malicious Package product, including the Malicious Package Identification API. We suggest re-scanning all projects which rely on any of these packages to determine if any were placed into production with vulnerable versions during the window between attack and discovery.

On September 8, 2025, a phishing campaign targeting a maintainer of the widely used ‘chalk’ package escalated into one of the most severe supply chain compromises observed in the npm ecosystem to date. Within approximately 16 minutes of gaining account access, attackers injected malicious code into at least 18 trusted JavaScript packages which, collectively, are downloaded over two billion times per week. [...] ‘chalk’, a popular Node.js library used for styling console output, became the distribution vector for cryptocurrency-draining malware. The injected code employed advanced evasion techniques to intercept wallet transactions and manipulate application behavior, enabling theft while concealing malicious activity from end users. results.title: npm debug / chalk Supply-Chain Attack: The Complete Guide
results.content:
What happened? Multiple popular npm packages (including debug, chalk, and core dependencies like ansi-styles, strip-ansi, supports-color) were published with malicious, browser-side code that silently intercepts crypto/web3 activity and rewrites payment destinations to attacker addresses.
 When? Malicious versions began appearing September 8, 2025 ~13:15 UTC, detected by Aikido.
 Scope: 18 packages, collectively >2B weekly downloads, making this a potentially far-reaching incident. [...] ## What Happened?

On September 8, 2025, new versions of 18 high-traffic packages were pushed to npm with obfuscated code that, when executed in a browser context, monitors and tampers with crypto/web3 flows. The malware hooks into network and wallet APIs, rewriting recipients and approval targets to attacker addresses — all while keeping the UI looking legitimate. 

The attack began with a successful phishing attack against a package maintainer via a fake npm support domain (npmjs.help).
